BBC 23 Nov 13:50

Former PMs are 'stuck in the past' on Brexit, Burnham says

Andy Burnham has said former prime ministers who have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate are \"stuck in the past\".

Baroness Theresa May and Rishi Sunak are the latest in a string of former Conservative leaders to criticise Burnham's approach.

But the PM said he would not listen to people who \"left Britain with a bad Brexit deal\".

It comes after Burnham agreed a deal with the EU, covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

At a summit on Friday, he also said that over the next 12 months both sides would \"brainstorm\" options for the UK's long-term relationship with the EU.

Burnham has previously suggested potential options for the future could include rejoining the customs union, the single market or a fresh referendum on full EU membership.

However, he has ruled out major changes to the UK-EU relationship before the next general election, saying he will stick to Labour's 2024 manifesto pledge not to return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement.

Asked about the criticism from his predecessors, Burnham told broadcasters: \"I'm not sure they're the people I'll be listening to here because they left Britain with a bad Brexit deal that has hit growth over the last decade, has lifted the cost of living, reduced opportunities for young people and of course the main one you could say, limited our ambition to control immigration.\"

He added: \"They're stuck in the past because they can't face up to the bad deal that they did...

\"I'm not a prime minister that's going to be stuck in the past. I want to lead Britain forward to a more hopeful future, get the economy growing again, get cost of living down for people, lower energy bills.

\"All of these things can be achieved by a more positive, constructive relationship with the European Union, our largest market.\"

Over the weekend, Baroness May, who spent three years negotiating an EU exit deal, told the BBC she was \"aghast\" Burnham could be considering rejoining.

She urged him to \"accept Brexit and move on\".

Sunak has also warned against reopening the \"divisive\" debate about rejoining the EU, telling Sky News it would be \"a huge distraction for government\".

Earlier this month, Boris Johnson, who negotiated the original Brexit deal as prime minister, said it was \"madness\" for Burnham to make Brexit his \"political priority\".

He told the Daily Telegraph, he believed the public would back Brexit again if Burnham forced another vote on the issue.

His Conservative predecessor Lord Cameron, who resigned as prime minister after losing the 2016 Brexit referendum, has also warned against \"another-decade long debate about whether we should be in or out\".

Meanwhile, former Labour Prime Minister Sir Tony Blair - who was a prominent opponent of leaving the EU - has said the UK should only rejoin the bloc if it reforms and allows more innovation on technology.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said she was concerned Burnham had \"opened a Pandora's Box\".

\"All of the old people having that debate are coming back out and relitigating. Five prime ministers, not just the Conservative ones, Tony Blair too, have told him that the rejoining of the EU conversation he's opened is not the right one,\" she said.

\"I just hope he's listening.\"

Nikki da Costa, who was director of legislative affairs under May and Johnson, pointed to the fact Burnham was not an MP when the government was negotiating the UK's exit from the EU.

\"Nobody that had lived through that would willingly plunge themselves into it without a very clear strategy not just a personal desire,\" she said.

Read more on the debate about the UK and the European Union

Neon signs made for Stanley Kubrick's Eyes Wide Shut film were among the props that went under the hammer in south-west London last week.

God's Own Junk Yard also had pieces made for Tomb Raider, Bridget Jones's Diary and Elton John for sale on Thursday at its workshop on Lots Road, Fulham.

Matthew Bracey, from the family-run business, says materials used to make traditional neon are becoming harder to find as LEDs take over.

He believes neon could be worth more than gold in 10 years' time.
